reason: Article 243K(1) vests the State Election Commission in a State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor; the source's own explanation says the same ('appointed by the Governor'), so the printed reasoning and the answer agree.
explanation: Under Article 243K(1) of the Constitution the State Election Commissioner — the officer who superintends the preparation of electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all Panchayat and Municipality elections — is appointed by the Governor of the state, and Article 243K(2) leaves his conditions of service and tenure to the Governor by rule. He can be removed only in the like manner and on the like grounds as a Judge of a High Court, and his service conditions cannot be varied to his disadvantage after appointment, which is what makes the office independent of the state executive. In Madhya Pradesh the tenure is six years or up to the age of 65, whichever is earlier. Do not confuse this officer with the Chief Election Commissioner of India, appointed by the President under Article 324, who conducts parliamentary and state Assembly elections.
key_concepts: Article 243K and 243ZA
State Election Commissioner appointed by the Governor
Removal on the grounds applicable to a High Court Judge

reason: The printed explanation dates the office to 18 September 2015, which is also the notification date recorded by NITI Aayog; the other three dates match no order creating the office.
explanation: The Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office (DMEO) was set up by the Government of India on 18 September 2015 as an attached office of NITI Aayog, by merging the erstwhile Programme Evaluation Office of the Planning Commission with the Independent Evaluation Office of the Prime Minister's Office. Its mandate is to institutionalise the application of monitoring and evaluation at every level of government policy and programme, to build the M&E ecosystem, and to support data-driven, citizen-centric and outcome-focused policy making; it also reviews flagship programmes for the governing council. The distractors move either the year (2016) or the month (December), so the office is best fixed in memory as an September-2015 creation of NITI Aayog.
key_concepts: Attached office of NITI Aayog
Merged the Programme Evaluation Office and the Independent Evaluation Office

reason: Of the four dates this paper prints (6, 7, 9 and 10 August 1942) only 9 August has any connection with the movement, and the printed explanation dates the arrests and the flag-hoisting to it. Several other printings of the same question carry '8th August, 1942' in this option slot, which is the date of the resolution itself.
explanation: The Quit India resolution was adopted by the All India Congress Committee at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942, after Jawaharlal Nehru moved it and Sardar Patel seconded it, and it is there that Gandhi gave the call 'Do or Die'. The movement broke out the following day: in the early hours of 9 August 1942 the entire Congress leadership — Gandhi, Nehru, Patel and the rest — was arrested and taken to unknown destinations, and the young leader Aruna Asaf Ali presided over the meeting and hoisted the Congress flag at the empty Gowalia Tank maidan. This paper therefore keys the start of the movement to 9 August 1942; 6, 7 and 10 August have nothing to do with it. Remember both dates: the resolution on 8 August, the mass 'August Kranti' from 9 August.
key_concepts: AICC session at Gowalia Tank, Bombay
Quit India resolution — 8 August 1942
Leaders arrested and movement begins — 9 August 1942
Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the Congress flag

reason: The Madhya Pradesh State Election Commission was constituted by a General Administration Department notification dated 1 February 1994 — the printed explanation says the same, and the state's own commission records that date.
explanation: Madhya Pradesh was the first state in India to constitute a State Election Commission after the 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments, and the Commission was constituted by a notification of the state General Administration Department dated 1 February 1994. It started functioning when the first State Election Commissioner, N. B. Lohani, assumed charge on 15 February 1994 — a date worth remembering, and deliberately not one of the options here. Its headquarters are at Bhopal, its motto is 'Every vote is precious, everybody is important', and under Articles 243K and 243ZA it conducts elections to Panchayats, municipalities and municipal corporations. The other three dates — 15 January, 15 March and 15 April 1994 — correspond to nothing in the Commission's history.

reason: MPPSC deleted this question, so no official key exists. Section 2(d) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 lists life, liberty, equality and dignity; education is not in that definition, which makes it the odd one out among the four options.
explanation: Section 2(d) of the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 defines 'human rights' as the rights relating to life, liberty, equality and dignity of the individual, guaranteed by the Constitution or embodied in the international covenants and enforceable by courts in India. Rights relating to life (Article 21), liberty (Articles 19 and 21) and equality (Articles 14 and 15) therefore fall inside the National Human Rights Commission's mandate, while the right to education does not appear in that statutory definition — it is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A and is governed by the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009, with its own enforcement route through the elementary-education provisions. MPPSC deleted this question, so there is no official key; the answer follows the wording of the Act rather than any published solution.

reason: MPPSC deleted this question, so no official key exists. The Bhimma are recorded as a section of the Gond tribe of Madhya Pradesh whose home is the Mandla-Dindori belt, and every source printing this question keys it to that pair.
explanation: The Bhimma (also written Bhoomia) appear in the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950 as one of the sections of the Gond tribe of Madhya Pradesh, and their home is the Gond belt of the eastern hills — Mandla and Dindori, on the Amarkantak plateau and the Maikal range, where the Scheduled Areas of the state lie. The other pairs are the home ground of different communities: the Baiga and the Gond of the Satpura side in Betul and Chhindwara, the Sahariya on the Rewa-Satna side, and the Bharia, Panika and Chatar Gond around Sidhi and Shahdol. For the exam it is enough to file Bhimma with the Mandla-Dindori Gond tract. Note that MPPSC deleted this question, so the answer rests on the tribe's documented distribution and not on an official key.

reason: MPPSC deleted this question, so no official key exists. The award instituted for writings on the cultural tradition and specialities of tribal life is the Veer Shankar Shah - Raghunath Shah National Award; the Thakkar Bapa award honours service to tribal communities, not literature.
explanation: The Veer Shankar Shah - Raghunath Shah National Award is given for writings on the cultural tradition and specialities of tribal life in Indian literature. It takes its name from the Gond father and son of the Ramnagar estate who led the revolt of 1857 across the Mandla and Amarkantak region and were hanged at Ramnagar in 1858, and a literary award in their names naturally looks for work that records tribal life. The other three do not fit: the Thakkar Bapa award recognises dedicated service to the tribal communities of Madhya Pradesh rather than writing about them, while the Rani Durgavati and Devi Ahilya awards honour women's achievement and public service generally. Because MPPSC deleted this question there is no official key; the answer follows what each award is instituted for.

reason: MPPSC deleted this question, so no official key exists. The standard elevations order the four peaks as Panchmarhi < Mahendragiri < Guru Shikhar < Anaimudi, which is option (iv), (ii), (i), (iii) — the code printed as option D.
explanation: By height the four peaks run as follows: Panchmarhi, whose highest point is Dhupgarh in the Satpura range of Madhya Pradesh, about 1,350 m; Mahendragiri in the Eastern Ghats of Odisha, about 1,501 m; Guru Shikhar on Mount Abu, the highest point of the Aravalli in Rajasthan, about 1,722 m; and Anaimudi in the Western Ghats of Kerala, about 2,695 m, the highest summit of peninsular India and of South India. Ascending order is therefore (iv), (ii), (i), (iii). Two of these are repeat favourites: Guru Shikhar for the Aravalli and Anaimudi for the Western Ghats, while Mahendragiri is the great name of the Eastern Ghats. Note that MPPSC deleted this question, so the ordering rests on the standard elevations rather than on an official key.
